reading.rtitle: The Starting Five, Ten Years Later
paras: In 2014 a school in Belo Horizonte won a national junior title with a starting five that everybody in the city knew by name. Ten years later a local journalist found all five of them and asked each one the same question: what do you miss? Nobody said winning. Two of them said the bus.

Rafael, who is now a civil engineer, used to be the tallest boy in every room he walked into, and he says that was an identity before it was a position. “I was the tall one. That is what I was for. Then I stopped growing at seventeen and everybody else did not, and I had to find out what else I was.” In retrospect, he says, the year that hurt was not the last one. It was the first one afterwards.

Two of the five would train before school as well as after it, which nobody asked them to do. Neither of those two still plays. The one who does play, every Sunday, in a league nobody watches, is the one who used to complain the most. “That is the joke of it,” he says. “I used to hate Tuesdays. Now Tuesday is the day I check whether we have a game.”

The journalist asked all five whether that era defined them. Four said yes and one refused the question. “Nostalgia is a trick,” she said — she coached the team for two seasons before moving away. “Those were the days is a sentence people say about a phase, not about a life. It shaped who I am. It does not describe who I am. The contrast is the whole point: if you look back on it and it still looks bigger than everything since, that is not a memory problem. That is a problem with everything since.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a junior team ten years on, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how junior basketball championships work in Brazil.
To show five people looking back at the same period, and to end on the one who refuses to let it explain her.
To argue that young athletes should keep playing after school.

items: All five of them said they missed winning.
Nobody said winning. Two of them said the bus.
Rafael says being tall was a position before it was an identity.
He says the opposite: it was an identity before it was a position.
The player who still plays every Sunday is the one who trained hardest.
The one who still plays is the one who used to complain the most. The two who trained before school do not play at all.
Rafael says the hardest year was the first one after he stopped.
In retrospect, he says, the year that hurt was not the last one but the first one afterwards.
The coach agreed that the era defined them.
She refused the question, and said it shaped her but does not describe her.
The coach says looking back is fine unless the past still looks bigger than the present.
She says if it still looks bigger than everything since, that is a problem with everything since.

items.situation: Say what Rafael was, not what he did, in one sentence.
tips: He used to be the tallest boy in every room.
A state, so only used to works. Would be is impossible here.

items.situation: Now say what two of them did every morning, in the nostalgic register.
tips: They would train before school as well as after it.
A repeated action, so would is available and it sounds like a story.

items.situation: Ask a question about the coach, using the question form.
tips: Did she use to play as well, or only coach?
Did plus use to, with no d on use.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: I would be nervous before every game.
tips: I used to be nervous before every game.
Nervous is a state. Would cannot carry a state.

items.situation: Say two things you used to do every day in Franca.
tips: I used to train five afternoons a week, and we would run before school.
Actions, so both structures are available. Mix them and it sounds natural.

items.situation: Now say one thing you used to BE, and one thing you are used to now.
tips: I used to be the youngest one on the court.
I am used to waking up at twenty to six. Two different structures, on purpose.

listenings.text: I did not answer him at the time because the question was wrong, so here is the answer now. He asked whether that era defined us. It did not. It shaped us, which is a different verb, and the difference matters more than it sounds. I used to think nostalgia was harmless. I do not any more. It is not that the memories are false. It is that memory keeps the Sunday and quietly throws away the Tuesday, and then you compare a life made of Tuesdays to a highlight reel and you lose, every time. Those were the days is a sentence about a phase. When somebody says it about a whole life, listen carefully, because they are usually telling you something about right now.

For two hundred years nostalgia was classified as an illness. Doctors wrote it up as a disorder of soldiers far from home, and they proposed treatments for it, some of them unpleasant. The modern research says almost the opposite. When people are asked to remember a period they loved, they come out of it measurably more optimistic, more generous and more willing to try something new. That is a strange result for an illness. The current explanation is that nostalgia is not about the past at all. It is a way of reminding yourself that you have been someone before, which is the evidence you need to believe you can be someone again. The people it damages are the ones who use it as a place to live rather than a place to visit.
